source: P² = a³ when the period is in years and the size of the orbit is in astronomical units.
Students think a planet twice as far out takes twice as long, missing that it also moves more slowly.

Kepler's second law covers one planet. In 1619 he found a rule that links them all: the farther a planet is from the Sun, the longer its year, in a precise way. It uses the fractional exponents you know: $P = a^{3/2}$.

Measure the period $P$ in years and the semi-major axis $a$ in AU, and for every planet $P^2 = a^3$. Two things stretch an outer planet's year. Its path is longer, in proportion to $a$. And gravity is weaker out there, so it moves more slowly: for circular orbits, speed goes as $1/\sqrt{a}$. Time is path divided by speed: $P \propto a \div \frac{1}{\sqrt{a}} = a^{3/2}$, so $P^2 \propto a^3$. Earth sets the units: $1$ AU and $1$ year make the constant $1$.
Kepler's third law: $P^2 = a^3$ ($P$ in years, $a$ in AU, for bodies orbiting the Sun). So $P = a^{3/2}$ and $a = P^{2/3}$. Twice as far means $2^{3/2} \approx 2.8$ times as long.
The two columns on the right agree: $P^2 = a^3$ (orbital data from NASA).
An orbit with $a = 2$ AU takes $2^{3/2} = 2.83$ years. On log scales, $\log P = \frac{3}{2}\log a$ is a straight line through all eight planets.
Jupiter's orbit has $a = 5.20$ AU. Find its period.
An asteroid orbits the Sun every $8$ years. How far out is it?
$a = \sqrt[3]{64} = 4$ AU: beyond the main asteroid belt, a little more than three-quarters of the way out to Jupiter.

A tempting guess is that a planet twice as far out takes twice as long. That forgets the second effect: it also moves more slowly. Check with $P^2 = a^3$: $a = 2$ gives $P = \sqrt{8} \approx 2.83$ years, not 2. Mars ($1.52$ AU) takes $1.88$ years, not $1.52$.
This form works only for objects orbiting the Sun, in years and AU. Newton's version works around any star or planet. Launch your own orbits in the Orbit Lab.
